name: Poetry
vendor: Poetry project (python-poetry), created by Sébastien Eustace
summary: A Python tool, written in Python, that resolves a project’s dependencies into `poetry.lock`, keeps a virtualenv per project and builds and publishes packages.
intro: Poetry keeps everything about a project in `pyproject.toml`. Since Poetry 2.0 (January 2025) that means the standard `[project]` table; older projects use `[tool.poetry]`. `poetry add pydantic` picks a caret range (`^2.14.0`, written as `>=2.14.0,<3.0.0`), resolves the whole dependency tree, installs it into the project’s virtualenv (by default under Poetry’s cache directory) and writes the exact versions and file hashes to `poetry.lock`, which covers every platform at once. Since 2.0 the lockfile also records which dependency group and environment markers each package belongs to. `poetry install` on another machine installs exactly those versions, `poetry build` makes wheels and sdists with the `poetry-core` build backend, and `poetry publish` uploads them. Development dependencies go into groups; since 2.2 (September 2025) Poetry also reads and writes the standard PEP 735 `[dependency-groups]` table.

Poetry itself is a Python application and must be installed in its own isolated environment, with pipx or the official installer, never into the project it manages. Version 2.1 added an experimental `poetry python install` that downloads standalone Python builds. Extras live in plugins: since 2.0, `poetry export` (which can write `pylock.toml` since 2.3) and `poetry shell` are no longer built in. The project is actively maintained; 2.5.0 shipped in September 2026.
strengths: Mature: dependency management, locking, virtualenvs, building and publishing in one tool since 2018
One lockfile for every platform, now with groups and markers recorded per package
Caught up with the standards: PEP 621 `[project]` metadata (2.0) and PEP 735 dependency groups (2.2)
A plugin system (since 1.2) for features the core leaves out, and projects can declare the plugins they need
limits: Resolution can be slow when packages don’t publish their metadata through PyPI’s JSON API: Poetry then downloads them to inspect, and its FAQ admits there is no way around it
Being written in Python means installing Poetry into its own environment, separate from the interpreter each project uses
Poetry 2.0 broke habits: `poetry shell` and `poetry export` moved to plugins and `poetry lock` stopped updating versions by default
`poetry.lock` is Poetry’s own format; the standard `pylock.toml` is only available through the export plugin

worksWith.how: manages dependencies and builds packages for

snippet.title: Add dependencies, lock them and reinstall from the lockfile (Poetry 2.4)
source: poetry new demo && cd demo        # [project] metadata, src layout, poetry-core backend
poetry add --group dev ruff       # lands in [dependency-groups] dev (PEP 735)
poetry check --lock               # All set!  (pyproject.toml and poetry.lock agree)

story: In 2018 a Python project typically spread its metadata over `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `requirements.txt`, `MANIFEST.in` and, for Pipenv users, a `Pipfile`. Sébastien Eustace, also the author of the Pendulum datetime library, released Poetry 0.1.0 on 28 February 2018 to replace all of them with a single `pyproject.toml`, a resolver and a lockfile.

Poetry 1.0 followed in December 2019, with Eustace thanking their employer at the time, PeopleDoc, for time to work on it. Version 1.2 (August 2022) added dependency groups, a new installer and an experimental plugin system, and later releases moved non-core commands such as `export` into plugins.

As standards for project metadata, dependency groups and lockfiles were adopted, Poetry followed them: the standard `[project]` table in 2.0 (January 2025), PEP 735 dependency groups in 2.2 (September 2025) and `pylock.toml` export in 2.3 (January 2026). It now competes with uv, which covers the same ground.

choices.why: One file replaced `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `requirements.txt`, `MANIFEST.in` and `Pipfile`, so dependencies, metadata and build settings could no longer drift apart.
`poetry add` writes `^2.14.0`, allowing any update that keeps the left-most non-zero digit, so projects pick up fixes without accepting the next breaking release.
`poetry.lock` is platform-independent, unlike the requirements files pip-tools locks for one platform, so teams on different operating systems share one file.
The plugin system (1.2) let users adapt Poetry without forking it, and let the maintainers move commands such as `export` and `shell` out of the core in 2.0.

timeline.text: 1.2: dependency groups, a new installer and plugins
2.0 adopts the standard `[project]` table; 2.2 adds PEP 735 dependency groups
2.3 exports `pylock.toml` via plugin; 2.5 adds a built-in uninstaller
